objectives.title: A joined-up plan with our neighbours
objectives.summary: An integrated Bus Service Improvement Plan across Sussex
objectives.description:
Lancing has 65 bus stops averaging 32.8 departures each on a weekday. South Portslade, four miles along the same coast road but on the Brighton & Hove side of the boundary, has 43 stops averaging 117.0. That is roughly three and a half times the service per stop, for a comparable seaside neighbourhood on the same corridor.

Three authorities plan buses along this coast: West Sussex, Brighton & Hove and East Sussex. The gap above is what that looks like from a bus stop.

Those figures are counted, not estimated. They come from the published timetable for a dated weekday, and the method, the denominators and the caveats are set out in full on the Route view's boundary evidence. The caveat that matters most is that this measures scheduled service rather than buses that ran, and that being near a council boundary is not on its own proof that the boundary caused the gap.

What a passenger meets is not a boundary. It is a bus that turns back, a ticket that stops being valid, and a timetable that thins out for no reason visible from the pavement.

We want West Sussex to work with Brighton & Hove City Council and East Sussex County Council on one integrated Bus Service Improvement Plan for the Sussex coast: a single network planned end to end, with shared targets for frequency, hours and through-ticketing, rather than three plans that each stop at a line on a map.
objectives.letter:
Buses along our stretch of coast are planned separately by West Sussex, Brighton & Hove and East Sussex, and it shows. The published timetables give Lancing far fewer buses per stop than South Portslade, four miles along the same coast road on the Brighton & Hove side.

I would like West Sussex County Council to work with Brighton & Hove City Council and East Sussex County Council on one Bus Service Improvement Plan for the Sussex coast, with shared targets for frequency, hours and through-ticketing.

objectives.title: More hours on the routes we already have
objectives.summary: Earlier mornings and later evenings on limited-frequency routes
objectives.description:
A shift starting at seven and a shift ending at eleven both fall outside what many Adur and Worthing routes run. A large number of them carry only a handful of journeys a day, with nothing early enough for the first and nothing late enough for the second. Care workers, hospital staff, hospitality workers and anyone whose hours do not fit an office day are left driving, paying for taxis, or turning the job down.

Adding journeys at each end of the day on routes that already exist is among the cheapest things that can be done for the network. The vehicles, the drivers' depots, the stops and the route registrations are all in place. What is missing is an hour at the start and an hour or two at the end.

The ask is that West Sussex County Council works with the operators to identify the limited-frequency routes where an earlier first bus and a later last bus would open up shift work, and funds those journeys where they are not commercially viable on their own.
objectives.letter:
Many routes in Adur and Worthing run only a handful of journeys a day, with nothing early enough for a seven o'clock shift and nothing late enough to get home from an evening one. Care workers, hospital staff and hospitality workers are left driving, paying for taxis or turning work down.

I would like West Sussex County Council to work with the operators on which routes most need an earlier first bus and a later last bus, and to fund those journeys where they are not commercially viable.

objectives.title: Express buses for commuters
objectives.summary: Faster peak-time links between Worthing and Brighton, and a second operator running them
objectives.description:
Getting between Worthing and Brighton at peak times is slow, and one company does almost all of it. Both problems have the same fix.

Brighton & Hove Buses stop at Shoreham. Across the Adur and Worthing corridor they serve 576 stops, but not one in Lancing or Worthing. Their westernmost stop is Dacre Gardens, and the 28 stops they reach beyond Shoreham are all on routes 2, 2B, 59 and 59A, running north up the Adur valley towards Steyning and Upper Beeding rather than west along the coast.

West of Shoreham there are 736 stops with a bus service. Compass reaches 395 of them and Stagecoach 386. Brighton & Hove reaches 28, all of them in the valley. Lancing and Worthing therefore sit on the edge of Brighton's network, served by everyone except the operator whose network they most need to reach. A Worthing passenger has no Brighton & Hove option at all, and no competitive alternative on the corridor.

Brighton & Hove served Lancing and Worthing within living memory. Bringing those services back west would give the coast a second operator, a choice of bus, and a direct link into the Brighton network that today needs a change and a second ticket.

There may also be a cheap way to make the existing service faster: split a frequent route so that at peak times every other journey runs express, calling only at the main stops. The attraction is that it could be done within the existing fleet, since a faster round trip can free the running time it needs. Whether it can depends on the route's cycle time, its layover and its peak vehicle requirement, and we have not seen those worked through. We are asking the operator and West Sussex County Council to evaluate it and publish the result, not asserting that it costs nothing.
objectives.letter:
Getting between Worthing and Brighton at peak times is slow, and one company runs almost every bus. Brighton & Hove Buses serve no stops in Lancing or Worthing, so there is no second operator on the corridor and no direct link into the Brighton network.

I would like the operators and West Sussex County Council to look at bringing Brighton & Hove services back west, and to evaluate running some peak journeys as express services calling only at the main stops.

objectives.title: Merge the Stagecoach DayRider zones
objectives.summary: One coastal DayRider covering Worthing and Brighton, at the £6 each already costs
objectives.description:
Stagecoach sells a Worthing DayRider and a Brighton DayRider at £6 each, and the two zones do not overlap anywhere. Of the stops Stagecoach serves, 361 sit in the Worthing zone and 186 in the Brighton zone, and not a single one sits in both. Every journey along the coast between the two towns therefore crosses a boundary.

For a simple return trip that boundary costs nothing extra today, because England's national fare cap holds a single at £3: two buses, £6, and no day ticket needed. The boundary bites the moment you need more than two journeys in a day: a school run, a shift with an errand on the way home, a day's work in the other town. Then you are buying a day ticket, and there is no day ticket for this stretch of coast. You buy both zones at £12, or a Gold DayRider valid across Hampshire, Surrey and Berkshire bought purely to travel between Worthing and Brighton.

Stagecoach sells that Gold ticket at £8.50 in its app; its published fares table effective 1 June 2026 lists it at £9. Against a merged coastal DayRider at the £6 each zone already costs, that is £2.50 to £3 a day, paid by people making one of the most ordinary journeys in the area. Stagecoach's Flexi5 bundle brings a regular traveller's cost down to £7.20 a day, which narrows the gap without closing it, and still requires buying network-wide coverage to cross one line.

One coastal DayRider covering both zones, priced at the same £6 the two separate tickets already cost. It adds no new mileage for the operator.
objectives.letter:
Stagecoach sells a Worthing DayRider and a Brighton DayRider at £6 each, and the two zones do not overlap, so every journey along the coast between the towns crosses a boundary. Anyone making more than two trips in a day has to buy both zones or a much wider Gold ticket.

I would like Stagecoach, with the support of West Sussex County Council, to offer one coastal DayRider covering both zones at the £6 each already costs.

objectives.title: One ticket for the whole coast
objectives.summary: Mutual ticket acceptance between operators, at day-ticket prices
objectives.description:
At 502 of the 1,633 stops in the Adur, Worthing and Brighton corridor, almost a third of them, more than one company's buses call. At those stops the bus that arrives first decides whether the ticket in your pocket is valid. A Stagecoach DayRider is not accepted on a Brighton & Hove or Metrobus service, so passengers either watch a bus go past and wait for the right livery, or pay twice for the same journey.

Half of this already exists. Metrovoyager is valid on Brighton & Hove services, and networkSAVER is valid on Metrobus within its zone. The gap is Stagecoach, which accepts nobody and is accepted by nobody. The all-operator South Downs Discovery Ticket does exist at £10, but it is priced and marketed as a day-out rover rather than a commuter fare, and it is not valid on the N700 or the N1.

What we want is mutual ticket acceptance across the corridor at ordinary day-ticket prices, so that a ticket bought for a journey is valid on whichever bus makes that journey.
objectives.letter:
At almost a third of the stops in the Adur, Worthing and Brighton corridor more than one company's buses call, but a ticket bought from one operator is often not valid on the next bus to arrive. Passengers either wait for the right livery or pay twice.

I would like the operators to accept each other's tickets across the corridor at ordinary day-ticket prices, as some of them already do with each other.

objectives.title: Night service that goes west
objectives.summary: Affordable late-night travel westward from Brighton, beyond the N700
objectives.description:
After the last daytime buses, travel westward out of Brighton depends almost entirely on one route, the N700. It runs along a narrow coastal corridor, it is expensive, and the ordinary day tickets most passengers already hold are not valid on it.

So an evening in Brighton ends early for anyone living in Adur or Worthing, or it ends in a taxi fare that costs more than the evening did. That falls hardest on the people least able to absorb it: hospitality and night-shift staff travelling home from work, and younger passengers without a car.

We are asking for more night service running west from Brighton into Adur and Worthing, at fares consistent with the daytime network rather than at a premium. At minimum, existing day tickets and passes should be honoured on the night services that already run.
objectives.letter:
After the daytime buses finish, getting home west from Brighton depends almost entirely on the N700, and the ordinary day tickets most passengers hold are not valid on it. An evening in Brighton ends early for people in Adur and Worthing, or ends in a taxi.

I would like more night service running west from Brighton at fares in line with the daytime network, and existing day tickets and passes honoured on the night buses that already run.

objectives.title: Accessible buses and stops for everyone
objectives.summary: Audio-visual next-stop information on every bus
objectives.description:
Every bus should announce and display the route, the direction of travel and the next stop. Without it, a passenger who cannot see the street or cannot hear the driver has no reliable way of knowing where they are, and people stop travelling independently.

This is the law, and the deadline has almost run out. The Public Service Vehicles (Accessible Information) Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/715) require audible and visible route, direction and next-stop information on local bus services, phased by vehicle age: vehicles first used from 1 October 2019 had to comply by 1 October 2024; those first used between October 2014 and September 2019 by 1 October 2025; and the remainder by 1 October 2026.

That last deadline is not a blanket rule about every older vehicle. The regulations carry published exemptions, and the Department for Transport maintains a current list of them (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/providing-accessible-information-onboard-local-bus-and-coach-services/current-exemptions-from-the-public-service-vehicles-accessible-information-regulations-2023). Some services and some vehicles are outside the requirement or have been granted more time. So the question to put to an operator is not "why is this old bus not compliant" but "which of your vehicles here are in scope, which are exempt, and on what date will the rest comply".

The ask is that operators confirm publicly which of their vehicles serving Adur and Worthing are compliant and which are not, with a date for the rest; and that the councils, as the bodies funding supported services and letting contracts, make compliance a condition of that funding.
objectives.letter:
The Public Service Vehicles (Accessible Information) Regulations 2023 require local buses to announce and display the route, direction and next stop, with the last phase due by 1 October 2026 and some vehicles exempt. Without it, passengers who cannot see the street or hear the driver stop travelling independently.

I would like the operators to confirm publicly which of their buses here comply and when the rest will, and the councils to make compliance a condition of the services they fund.

objectives.title: Clear, real-time information everywhere
objectives.summary: E-Ink live displays at every stop and one real-time app across operators
objectives.description:
Most bus stops in Adur and Worthing still carry only a paper timetable. If the bus is late, cancelled or diverted, there is no way to find that out while standing at the stop, and a passenger without a smartphone has no way of finding it out at all. Waiting twenty minutes for a bus that is never coming is one of the things that persuades people never to try the bus again.

Two things would fix most of it. First, E-Ink live departure displays at as many stops as possible: they are far cheaper to install and run than traditional powered signs, need no mains connection, are readable in daylight, and are already in use elsewhere in West Sussex. Second, real-time data published openly and completely by every operator, so that any app (including the councils' own) can show the whole network rather than one company's part of it, with fares and disruption information included.

We want a costed programme for live displays at the busiest stops, prioritising interchanges and stops serving hospitals, schools and employment sites, and a requirement that operators publish complete, accurate real-time and fares data for the whole corridor.
objectives.letter:
Most bus stops in Adur and Worthing still have only a paper timetable, so there is no way to find out at the stop whether a bus is late, cancelled or diverted, and no way at all without a smartphone.

I would like a costed programme of low-power live departure displays at the busiest stops and interchanges, and a requirement that operators publish complete, accurate real-time and fares data for the whole corridor.
